answer.why: As an insider, 'Confirmed & Substantive' made me laugh straight away because it is exactly the phrase you chase in the service: confirmation in appointment, then substantive rank after acting. It signals the makers know how careers actually move, and that the humour will be in the details. 'Minister Salary' feels like the obvious headline-bait, and the salary benchmark debate is something I live with already, so I would not need a game for it. But I would be a bit worried that only insiders would get the title.
answer.expect_minister_salary: Going on the name alone, a satirical, slightly cynical game about the ministerial pay debate: chasing the big number, probably a bit of a gag about benchmarks and the top-of-the-ladder jackpot. Punchy and easy for any Singaporean to get, but I would expect it to be shallow and political-lite, more about the payoff than the climb, and I would wonder if it was mocking the system or the people in it.
answer.expect_confirmed_substantive: A drier, more insider game about the grind of a career: probation, confirmation, acting appointments, waiting to be made substantive, appraisal wording. I would expect it to be specific, slightly bureaucratic and funny in a deadpan way, and to reward people who know how the service really works. Outsiders might find the name opaque or dull, though, and it reads like an HR circular, which is half the joke.

agent.why: I read it out last time and trust held, so dodging it now would undo that and officers would notice at once.
agent.confused_by: Pay shows $39.72M beside an annual package of $2.5M, and I can't tell which is the real figure.
agent.note: The Townhall has come round again, so the game is recycling events; same as Y33.
agent.remember: Y35: Townhall again; read out the top workload question and answered it directly, same as Y33. STAND 86 (-1). Still watching whether the Y29 passed question returns.

best_moment.what: Nominating the quiet officer for PSLP instead of myself, then having her quietly put my name forward in Y12. It felt like how favours really travel in the service: unspoken and years later.

worst_moment.what: The second workload Townhall, which was a repeat of Y33 with a STAND change of -1. By then the loop of Townhall, fix something nobody asked for and PQ answer had gone flat.

skip_year.why: A quiet year where I repeated a choice I had already made and nothing new happened. I could have tapped straight through.

answer.held_back_by: Nothing held me back, since I ended as PM. If anything slowed me it was the STAND slide, which I suspect was a drift mechanic or the Y29 passed question rather than my candour. I never saw it explained.
answer.ending_fair_why: I reached PM with Integrity 100 after mostly sensible and occasionally principled choices, and the card said the formula was published so nobody could say they were not told. That fits the real system. I never saw the Y4 consultants choice or the Y29 Cabinet question pay off, though, so some threads just stopped.
answer.chase_next: I would chase an ending where I tempted myself: take the Y29 Cabinet question the other way, or let the Y4 integrity dip surface in a background check, to see whether the game punishes a compromise or only hints at it.
answer.play_again_why: The middle and late years got repetitive, with the same PQ and Townhall beats, and I would want a break before trying a different temperament.

tone_breaks.line: Game's ages, grades and pay are inconsistent
tone_breaks.note: Ages, grades and pay did not line up with how real careers move. I stopped trusting the numbers and ignored them.

tone_breaks.line: The formula pays you twice the entry-grade minister's salary
tone_breaks.note: I could not tell whether this was meant to be accurate. The real benchmark is not framed that way, and PM pay as a simple multiple read oddly to an insider.

answer.title_fit_why: What I enjoyed was the slow, procedural, appraisal-and-favour part of the work, not the salary, and the salary card was the least interesting part of the ending.
